lessons.lessonTitle: Why Cells Need Membranes
lessons.examTip: Students describe the membrane as a wall — missing that it's a dynamic, selective filter; the hydrophobic core blocks charged/polar molecules but not small nonpolar ones like O2 and CO2

lessons.lessonTitle: How Cells Move Substances Without Using Energy
topics: Concentration gradient as the driving force
lessons.examTip: Students say water moves toward 'lower concentration' — water moves toward HIGHER solute concentration (lower water potential); confusing solute concentration with water concentration is the #1 osmosis error

lessons.lessonTitle: When Cells Must Spend Energy to Move Things
lessons.examTip: Students treat active transport as simply 'moving against a gradient' without explaining WHY — the Na+/K+ pump moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP, creating both concentration AND charge gradients

lessons.lessonTitle: What Mitochondria Actually Do (Not Just 'Powerhouse')
topics: ATP yield and where each stage occurs
Why oxygen is the final electron acceptor
lessons.examTip: Students memorize '36 ATP' without understanding that most ATP comes from the ETC (chemiosmosis), not Krebs — glycolysis produces only 2 net ATP; exam questions target WHERE in the cell each stage occurs

lessons.lessonTitle: How Cells Capture Light Energy
topics: Light reactions (photosystem II → I, ATP and NADPH)
Why C4 and CAM plants do it differently
lessons.examTip: Students think photosynthesis and respiration are opposites — they share intermediates (both use the ETC); students also confuse where O2 is produced (light reactions, from water splitting) vs. where CO2 is used (Calvin cycle)

lessons.lessonTitle: How One Cell Becomes Two (and Why It Must Be Precise)
topics: Mitosis: PMAT stages and chromosome behavior
Cytokinesis differences in plant vs. animal cells
lessons.examTip: Students say 'chromosomes duplicate during mitosis' — DNA replication happens in S phase (interphase), BEFORE mitosis begins; during mitosis chromosomes condense and separate, not replicate

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Meiosis Produces Variation, Not Just Gametes
topics: Comparing meiosis I vs. meiosis II outcomes
lessons.examTip: Students confuse meiosis I and II: meiosis I separates HOMOLOGOUS chromosomes (reducing from 2n to n); meiosis II separates SISTER CHROMATIDS — meiosis II looks like mitosis but starts with haploid cells

lessons.lessonTitle: How Cells Coordinate Their Own Death and Division
topics: Cancer as loss of checkpoint control
lessons.examTip: Students say cancer is 'too much growth' without specifying the mechanism — cancer results from BOTH proto-oncogene activation (accelerator stuck on) AND tumor suppressor mutation (brakes cut); both must be explained

lessons.lessonTitle: Why DNA's Shape Determines Its Function
topics: Double helix: antiparallel strands, base pairing rules
Why A-T has 2 H-bonds and G-C has 3
lessons.examTip: Students write DNA replication as symmetric — the leading strand is synthesized continuously, but the lagging strand requires Okazaki fragments because DNA polymerase only reads 3'→5' and builds 5'→3'

lessons.lessonTitle: How DNA Becomes Protein (The Full Path)
lessons.examTip: Students confuse template strand direction — the template strand is read 3'→5', so mRNA is synthesized 5'→3'; codon on mRNA and anticodon on tRNA are antiparallel, not identical

lessons.lessonTitle: What Mutations Actually Do to a Protein
topics: Why location of mutation matters more than type
lessons.examTip: Students think any mutation is harmful — silent mutations change the codon but not the amino acid (degeneracy of genetic code); a missense mutation in an active site is catastrophic, but in a non-functional region may be neutral

lessons.lessonTitle: Predicting Offspring Traits the Right Way
topics: Mendel's laws: segregation and independent assortment
lessons.examTip: Students apply independent assortment to genes on the SAME chromosome — linked genes violate independent assortment; crossing over can separate linked genes, but they're not inherited at the expected 9:3:3:1 ratio

lessons.lessonTitle: When Simple Dominance Doesn't Apply
lessons.examTip: Students treat codominance and incomplete dominance as the same — codominance: BOTH phenotypes fully expressed (AB blood type shows both A and B); incomplete dominance: a BLEND (red + white = pink); these produce different phenotypes

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Sex-Linked Traits Skip Generations
topics: Carrier females and affected males ratio
lessons.examTip: Students think X-linked traits only affect males — carrier females (X^A X^a) are unaffected but pass the allele to 50% of sons; X-linked dominant traits affect females MORE because they have two X chromosomes

lessons.lessonTitle: How Gene Expression Is Turned On and Off
topics: Eukaryotic gene regulation: enhancers and silencers
lessons.examTip: Students flip lac operon logic — lactose REMOVES the repressor (induces transcription); when glucose is absent AND lactose is present, transcription is maximal; students miss that both conditions must be met for full expression

lessons.lessonTitle: Biotechnology: How We Read and Edit DNA
lessons.examTip: Students say gel electrophoresis separates by 'size' — smaller fragments move FARTHER from the well (toward positive end); students reverse this, placing large bands at the bottom instead of the top

lessons.lessonTitle: What Darwin Actually Argued (and What He Didn't)
topics: Natural selection: variation, heritability, differential reproduction
Fitness as reproductive success, not strength
Common descent vs. progressive evolution myth
lessons.examTip: Students say organisms 'adapt' intentionally — natural selection acts on existing HERITABLE variation, not on need; an organism cannot generate a useful mutation because it needs one

lessons.lessonTitle: The Evidence That Species Change Over Time
topics: Molecular evidence: DNA comparison and cytochrome c
lessons.examTip: Students confuse homologous and analogous structures — homologous structures share COMMON ANCESTRY (bat wing/human arm = same bones, different function); analogous structures share FUNCTION but NOT ancestry (bat wing/butterfly wing)

lessons.lessonTitle: How Populations Evolve (Not Individuals)
lessons.examTip: Students calculate p and q correctly but misidentify which genotype frequency they need — q² = frequency of homozygous recessive; q = √(q²), then p = 1 - q; always start with q² from the given phenotype data

lessons.lessonTitle: Mechanisms That Change Allele Frequencies
topics: Gene flow and mutation as evolutionary forces
Natural selection types: directional, stabilizing, disruptive
lessons.examTip: Students rank natural selection as the strongest evolutionary force — in small populations, GENETIC DRIFT can overpower selection, fixing harmful alleles by chance; the bottleneck effect is a common FRQ setup

lessons.lessonTitle: How New Species Form
lessons.examTip: Students say geographic isolation = speciation — geographic isolation leads to genetic divergence, but speciation only occurs when REPRODUCTIVE ISOLATION develops; you can have allopatric populations that can still interbreed

lessons.lessonTitle: Reading the Tree of Life
topics: How to determine most recent common ancestor
lessons.examTip: Students read cladograms by looking at branch tips rather than branching points — the most recent common ancestor is found at the NODE where two lineages diverge, not at a tip; outgroup roots the tree

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Energy Is Lost at Every Trophic Level
topics: Biomass vs. energy vs. number pyramids
Why food chains rarely exceed 4–5 levels
lessons.examTip: Students invert pyramid of biomass in aquatic ecosystems — in open ocean, phytoplankton (producers) have LOWER biomass than zooplankton because phytoplankton reproduce so fast; inverted biomass pyramids are a recurring trick question

lessons.lessonTitle: How Nutrients Cycle While Energy Flows One Way
topics: Carbon cycle: key reservoirs and fluxes
lessons.examTip: Students say nitrogen fixation is done by plants — only certain bacteria (Rhizobium in root nodules, free-living Azotobacter) fix N2 into NH3; plants absorb fixed nitrogen as NO3- or NH4+, they cannot fix it themselves

lessons.lessonTitle: How Population Size Is Controlled
lessons.examTip: Students confuse the J-curve and S-curve — J-curve = exponential growth (no resource limits); S-curve = logistic growth (slows as population approaches K); the inflection point of the S-curve is at K/2, where growth rate is maximum

lessons.lessonTitle: Species Interactions: Who Wins and Who Loses
lessons.examTip: Students describe commensalism as 'both benefit slightly' — commensalism is (+/0): one benefits, the other is UNAFFECTED; mutualism is (+/+); students must be precise about the 0 in commensalism

lessons.lessonTitle: How Ecosystems Recover and Change Over Time
lessons.examTip: Students say the climax community is permanent — disturbance ecology shows ecosystems are dynamic; fire-adapted communities (chaparral) REQUIRE periodic disturbance to maintain their climax state; no ecosystem is truly at equilibrium

lessons.lessonTitle: Biodiversity: Why It Matters and What Threatens It
topics: Island biogeography: area and isolation effects
lessons.examTip: Students treat species richness as the only measure of biodiversity — an ecosystem with 100 species all at equal abundance (high evenness) is more diverse than one where 1 species dominates 90%; both dimensions matter

lessons.lessonTitle: How the Nervous System Processes and Responds
lessons.examTip: Students say sodium rushes IN to repolarize — sodium rushes in to DEPOLARIZE; potassium rushes OUT to repolarize; the Na+/K+ pump then restores resting potential; these three steps are all distinct and frequently tested separately

lessons.lessonTitle: How Hormones Control the Body's Long-Term Responses
lessons.examTip: Students confuse positive and negative feedback — negative feedback RESISTS change and maintains homeostasis (thermoregulation, blood glucose); positive feedback AMPLIFIES a change to completion (childbirth contractions, blood clotting)

lessons.lessonTitle: How the Immune System Distinguishes Self from Non-Self
lessons.examTip: Students say antibodies kill pathogens directly — antibodies FLAG antigens for destruction (opsonization) but do not kill; cytotoxic T cells directly kill infected cells; these are separate arms of adaptive immunity

lessons.lessonTitle: How the Heart and Lungs Work as a Single System
topics: Cardiac cycle: systole, diastole, AV/SL valves
Gas exchange in alveoli: diffusion driving forces
lessons.examTip: Students say deoxygenated blood is blue — blood is always red (oxyhemoglobin = bright red, deoxyhemoglobin = dark red); the blue appearance of veins is due to light absorption through skin, not the blood color

lessons.lessonTitle: How the Body Regulates Water and Waste
topics: ADH and aldosterone in water balance
lessons.examTip: Students say the kidney filters and then excretes everything filtered — 99% of filtered water and most solutes are REABSORBED; only a small fraction becomes urine; the nephron is primarily a recovery system, not an excretion system

lessons.lessonTitle: Human Reproduction and Embryonic Development
lessons.examTip: Students think oogenesis and spermatogenesis are parallel — spermatogenesis produces 4 functional sperm per meiosis; oogenesis produces 1 egg + 3 polar bodies per meiosis; unequal cytokinesis concentrates cytoplasm in the egg

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Atoms Are Mostly Empty Space (And What That Means)
topics: Rutherford's nuclear model vs. Thomson's plum pudding
Protons, neutrons, electrons: location and mass
Nuclear charge as the identity of an element
lessons.examTip: Students write atomic number = number of neutrons — atomic number = number of PROTONS; neutrons = mass number − atomic number; this error cascades into every electron configuration question

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Electrons Exist in Energy Levels, Not Orbits
topics: Quantum mechanical model: orbitals as probability clouds
Quantum numbers: n, l, ml, ms
lessons.examTip: Students write electron configurations by memorizing '1s 2s 2p...' without applying the Aufbau diagonal rule — the 4s orbital fills BEFORE 3d (lower energy), but 3d is listed before 4s in orbital notation

lessons.lessonTitle: How Electron Configuration Predicts Periodic Trends
topics: Ionization energy, atomic radius, electronegativity trends
Why trends reverse at filled/half-filled subshells
lessons.examTip: Students say 'ionization energy always increases across a period' — IE dips at group 3 (2p¹ has higher energy than 2s²) and at group 6 (pairing in 2p⁴ causes repulsion, easier to remove); oxygen has LOWER IE than nitrogen

lessons.lessonTitle: What Isotopes and Atomic Mass Really Tell Us
lessons.examTip: Students round atomic mass to find neutron count — atomic mass on the periodic table is a WEIGHTED AVERAGE, not the mass of any single atom; use the most abundant isotope's mass number to find neutrons

lessons.lessonTitle: How Light and Matter Exchange Energy
topics: Photoelectric effect: photon particle model of light
lessons.examTip: Students use E = hν with wavelength instead of frequency — E is proportional to FREQUENCY (ν), inversely proportional to wavelength (λ); high frequency = high energy = short wavelength; UV has MORE energy than infrared

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Metals Give Away Electrons and What That Creates
topics: Ionic bond formation: electron transfer and lattice energy
Lattice energy trend: charge and size
lessons.examTip: Students confuse ionic bond strength with electronegativity difference — lattice energy (ionic bond strength) depends on ION CHARGE and ION SIZE; MgO has higher lattice energy than NaCl because Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ have higher charges

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Nonmetals Share Electrons (And How to Draw It)
topics: Covalent bond: electron sharing and bond order
Lewis dot structures: octet rule and formal charge
lessons.examTip: Students minimize formal charges by guessing rather than calculating — formal charge = valence electrons − nonbonding electrons − ½(bonding electrons); the correct Lewis structure minimizes formal charge, and negative formal charge goes on the more electronegative atom

lessons.lessonTitle: How Molecular Shape Controls Everything
topics: VSEPR theory: electron domain geometry vs. molecular geometry
Bond angles and lone pair compression
lessons.examTip: Students name electron domain geometry instead of molecular geometry — 'tetrahedral electron geometry with 2 lone pairs' gives a BENT molecular geometry; the exam asks for molecular geometry, which ignores lone pairs when naming shape

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Some Molecules Are Polar and Others Aren't
topics: Why CO2 is nonpolar despite polar bonds
lessons.examTip: Students say any molecule with polar bonds is polar — CO2, BF3, and CCl4 have polar bonds but are NONPOLAR overall because the dipoles cancel due to symmetry; must assess both bond polarity AND molecular geometry

lessons.lessonTitle: What Determines If a Solid Will Melt Easily
lessons.examTip: Students break intramolecular bonds to explain boiling — boiling/melting involves overcoming INTERMOLECULAR FORCES, not breaking covalent bonds; HF has stronger H-bonds than HCl despite F-H bond being weaker than nothing students expect

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Metallic Bonds Explain All Metal Properties
topics: Electrical and thermal conductivity explained by delocalized electrons
Malleability vs. brittleness: metals vs. ionic solids
lessons.examTip: Students attribute metal conductivity to 'loosely held electrons' without specifying they are DELOCALIZED — ionic solids can conduct when melted or dissolved (ions move), but metals conduct in solid state because electrons move freely

lessons.lessonTitle: Why the Mole Is the Chemist's Dozen
topics: Avogadro's number and the mole concept
Converting between mass, moles, and particles
lessons.examTip: Students divide by molar mass when they should multiply and vice versa — always set up dimensional analysis with units canceling; if you want grams → moles, divide by molar mass (g/mol becomes a divisor)

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Balance Equations Without Changing the Chemistry
topics: Conservation of mass in chemical equations
Balancing by inspection: polyatomics as units
Why subscripts cannot be changed to balance
lessons.examTip: Students change subscripts to balance — H2O2 ≠ H2O; changing subscripts changes the SUBSTANCE; only coefficients in front of formulas can be adjusted; this is the most fundamental balancing error

lessons.lessonTitle: How the Mole Ratio Connects Reactants to Products
lessons.examTip: Students forget to use the mole ratio — they convert reactant to moles then convert directly to grams of product using the wrong molar mass; the mole ratio from the balanced equation MUST be applied between reactant moles and product moles

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Find the Ingredient That Runs Out First
topics: Why comparing moles, not grams, identifies the limit
lessons.examTip: Students identify the limiting reactant as 'whichever has fewer grams' — you must convert to moles and compare using the STOICHIOMETRIC RATIO, not raw mass; a larger mass can still be the limiting reactant

lessons.lessonTitle: Reading a Molecular Formula to Get Empirical and Molecular Formulas
lessons.examTip: Students round elemental ratios too aggressively — if C:H:O comes out 1:2.67:1, multiply all by 3 to get 3:8:3 (not round 2.67 to 3); ratios ending in .33 or .67 signal × 3; .5 signals × 2

lessons.lessonTitle: What Heat and Temperature Actually Measure
topics: Heat (q) vs. temperature (T): energy vs. average KE
lessons.examTip: Students apply q = mcΔT using the wrong mass — in a coffee cup calorimeter, the mass is the SOLUTION (or water), not the substance being tested; and q_rxn = −q_cal (equal and opposite sign)

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Calculate Energy Change in a Reaction
topics: Enthalpy of reaction (ΔH): exothermic vs. endothermic
Hess's Law: path independence of enthalpy
lessons.examTip: Students apply Hess's Law by adding equations without reversing signs — when a reaction is REVERSED, ΔH changes sign; when multiplied by n, ΔH is multiplied by n; both manipulations must be applied simultaneously

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Some Reactions Happen Spontaneously and Others Don't
topics: Gibbs free energy: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS
lessons.examTip: Students say a reaction is spontaneous if ΔH < 0 — spontaneity requires ΔG < 0, which depends on BOTH ΔH and ΔS; an endothermic reaction (ΔH > 0) can be spontaneous at high T if ΔS > 0

lessons.lessonTitle: How Energy Changes at Phase Boundaries
topics: Heat of fusion vs. heat of vaporization
Why ΔHvap >> ΔHfus for most substances
lessons.examTip: Students calculate heat during a phase change using q = mcΔT — during a phase change, TEMPERATURE IS CONSTANT; use q = m × ΔH_fusion or ΔH_vaporization; q = mcΔT applies only when temperature IS changing

lessons.lessonTitle: What Controls How Fast a Reaction Goes
topics: Collision theory: energy and orientation requirements
Catalysts: lowering Ea without changing ΔH
lessons.examTip: Students say a catalyst increases reaction rate by 'providing energy' — catalysts lower ACTIVATION ENERGY by providing an alternative pathway; they are not consumed and do not change the enthalpy of reaction (ΔH stays the same)

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Write Rate Laws from Experiments (Not Equations)
topics: Determining order from initial rate data
Integrated rate laws for first and second order
lessons.examTip: Students write rate laws from balanced equations — rate law orders CANNOT be determined from stoichiometry; they must be determined EXPERIMENTALLY by comparing initial rate data when one concentration is varied

lessons.lessonTitle: What Equilibrium Actually Means (Rates, Not Amounts)
topics: Dynamic equilibrium: forward rate = reverse rate
Why pure solids and liquids are excluded from Keq
lessons.examTip: Students write Keq including solid and liquid concentrations — pure solids and pure liquids have CONSTANT concentrations (activity = 1) and are excluded from the expression; water in aqueous reactions is excluded

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Predict Which Way a Reaction Will Shift
topics: Le Chatelier's principle: stress and response
Q vs. K comparison to predict shift direction
Effect of temperature on Keq value (not just shift)
lessons.examTip: Students say adding a catalyst shifts equilibrium — a catalyst speeds up BOTH forward and reverse reactions equally; it reaches equilibrium faster but does NOT shift the equilibrium position or change Keq

lessons.lessonTitle: Acid-Base Equilibrium: What pH Really Measures
topics: Strong vs. weak acids: complete vs. partial dissociation
lessons.examTip: Students set up weak acid ICE tables then forget to check if the approximation (x << [HA]₀) is valid — if x/[HA]₀ > 5%, the quadratic must be solved; blindly using the approximation when invalid gives wrong pH

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Assign and Track Electron Bookkeeping (Oxidation States)
topics: Oxidation state rules: O = −2, H = +1, sum rules
Oxidizing agent vs. reducing agent — which is which
lessons.examTip: Students confuse the oxidizing agent with the species being oxidized — the OXIDIZING AGENT causes oxidation in another species but is ITSELF REDUCED; the reducing agent is oxidized; always identify both the agent and what happens to it

lessons.lessonTitle: How Galvanic Cells Convert Chemistry to Electricity
topics: Salt bridge function: maintaining charge neutrality
Cell notation: anode | solution || solution | cathode
lessons.examTip: Students reverse anode and cathode in galvanic cells — in galvanic (voltaic) cells, ANODE is negative and CATHODE is positive (opposite of electrolytic cells); mnemonic: Red Cat / An Ox (reduction at cathode, oxidation at anode)

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Calculate Cell Voltage and Spontaneity
topics: Relationship between E°cell, ΔG°, and Keq
lessons.examTip: Students multiply E° values by stoichiometric coefficients — standard reduction potentials are INTENSIVE properties (they don't scale with moles); only ΔG° and Keq scale; E°cell stays the same regardless of how many electrons are transferred

lessons.lessonTitle: How Electrolytic Cells Force Non-Spontaneous Reactions
topics: Faraday's law: moles of electrons and product mass
lessons.examTip: Students forget to convert coulombs to moles of electrons in Faraday's law problems — moles of e⁻ = charge(C) / 96,485 (C/mol); then use stoichiometry of the half-reaction; skipping the conversion to moles is the most common error

lessons.lessonTitle: The Difference Between How Fast and How Much (Speed vs. Velocity)
lessons.examTip: Students calculate average speed as (v₁ + v₂)/2 — this only works if acceleration is constant; average velocity = total displacement / total time, which is always correct; these give different answers for non-uniform motion

lessons.lessonTitle: What Constant Acceleration Really Looks Like
topics: Kinematic equations: v = v₀ + at, x = v₀t + ½at², v² = v₀² + 2ax
Graphs: slope of x-t is v, slope of v-t is a
Free fall: a = −9.8 m/s² always downward
lessons.examTip: Students use g = +9.8 m/s² and then wonder why answers are wrong — pick a consistent positive direction; if upward is positive, acceleration due to gravity is −9.8 m/s²; sign errors on g cause wrong answers on every free-fall problem

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Horizontal and Vertical Motion Are Independent
topics: Range, max height, and time of flight equations
Launch angle optimization: 45° maximizes range on level ground
lessons.examTip: Students think a horizontally launched projectile falls slower because it moves forward — horizontal velocity has NO effect on vertical fall; both a dropped ball and a horizontally thrown ball hit the ground at the same time from the same height

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Add Vectors That Aren't in a Straight Line
topics: Vector components: Ax = A cos θ, Ay = A sin θ
lessons.examTip: Students use the angle measured from the wrong reference axis — always specify the angle as measured from the x-axis (or explicitly state from which axis); θ in Ax = A cos θ is measured from the POSITIVE x-axis, not the vertical

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Objects Don't Naturally Stop Moving
topics: Newton's First Law: inertia and reference frames
Friction as an external force, not a natural tendency
lessons.examTip: Students say objects slow down because 'they run out of force' — Newton's 1st Law says objects in motion STAY in motion unless acted on by a net external force; friction is the external force causing deceleration, not nature

lessons.lessonTitle: How Force, Mass, and Acceleration Are Exactly Connected
topics: Free body diagrams: all forces on ONE object
Normal force and tension as constraint forces
lessons.examTip: Students draw forces on multiple objects in one free body diagram — FBDs must show forces on ONE object only; the normal force on a block on a ramp is perpendicular to the ramp surface, NOT straight up

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Action-Reaction Pairs Never Cancel Each Other
topics: Newton's Third Law: equal and opposite force pairs
Why Newton's 3rd law pairs act on DIFFERENT objects
lessons.examTip: Students say the book on a table is in equilibrium because 'gravity equals normal force — they're action-reaction pairs' — the normal force and gravity are NOT a Newton's 3rd law pair (they act on the same object); the N3 pair of gravity on book is gravity on Earth from book

lessons.lessonTitle: How Friction Works — and When to Use Which Equation
topics: Static vs. kinetic friction: fs ≤ μsN, fk = μkN
lessons.examTip: Students apply kinetic friction to a stationary object — use STATIC friction (up to maximum fs = μsN) when the object is not moving; kinetic friction applies only WHILE sliding; the maximum static friction is GREATER than kinetic

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Objects Moving in Circles Must Have Inward Force
topics: Centripetal acceleration: ac = v²/r toward center
Centripetal force as net inward force (not a new force)
Why 'centrifugal force' is not real in inertial frames
lessons.examTip: Students add centrifugal force to their free body diagrams — centrifugal force does NOT exist in inertial frames; centripetal force is the NET result of REAL forces (tension, gravity, normal) pointing inward; never draw it as a separate force

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Work Is Not the Same as Effort
topics: Zero work: perpendicular force, no displacement
lessons.examTip: Students say gravity does no work on a pendulum — gravity does positive work on the downswing (force and displacement both downward) and negative work on the upswing; only centripetal force does ZERO work (always perpendicular to motion)

lessons.lessonTitle: How Energy Is Stored and Released in Conservative Systems
topics: Gravitational PE = mgh, Spring PE = ½kx²
lessons.examTip: Students use h = 0 inconsistently in the same problem — choose a reference height and KEEP IT; if you set the lowest point as h = 0, then use that same h = 0 for both sides of the energy equation

lessons.lessonTitle: Where Does Energy Go When Friction Is Present?
topics: Thermal energy generated by friction: Eth = fk × d
lessons.examTip: Students forget that the distance in Eth = fkd is the SLIDING distance between surfaces — for a block pulled up a ramp, it's the length of the ramp, not the vertical height; these are different and using the wrong one gives wrong answers

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Momentum Is Harder to Change Than Speed
lessons.examTip: Students think kinetic energy is conserved in all collisions — KE is conserved ONLY in elastic collisions; in inelastic collisions, KE is converted to internal energy (heat, deformation); momentum is ALWAYS conserved if no external forces act

lessons.lessonTitle: What Actually Moves in a Wave (It's Not the Medium)
topics: Wave parameters: amplitude, wavelength, frequency, speed
lessons.examTip: Students say 'the water moves forward in a water wave' — water molecules in a transverse wave move PERPENDICULAR to wave propagation, not forward; a floating duck bobs up and down, not horizontally toward shore

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Waves Interfere and What the Patterns Mean
topics: Superposition principle: constructive and destructive interference
lessons.examTip: Students think destructive interference destroys energy — energy is REDISTRIBUTED, not destroyed; where destructive interference occurs, the energy reappears at other locations (nodes have zero displacement but the energy is at antinodes)

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Strings and Pipes Produce Only Certain Frequencies
topics: Standing waves in strings: fn = nv/2L
Why closed pipes only produce odd harmonics
lessons.examTip: Students apply the string formula to closed pipes — a closed pipe (one end open, one closed) has a NODE at the closed end and ANTINODE at the open end; fundamental = v/4L (not v/2L); only odd harmonics are present

lessons.lessonTitle: Why a Moving Source Changes the Pitch You Hear
topics: Doppler effect: source approaching vs. receding
Why the observer hears higher f as source approaches
lessons.examTip: Students flip the Doppler formula numerator and denominator — use f' = f × (v ± v_observer)/(v ∓ v_source); upper signs when approaching (increase), lower when receding (decrease); observer motion affects numerator, source motion affects denominator

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Like Charges Repel and What Controls the Force
topics: Electric field: E = F/q (force per unit charge)
Field lines: direction, density, and interpretation
lessons.examTip: Students double the force when charge is doubled and distance is also doubled — Coulomb's Law has r², so doubling r DECREASES force by 4×; doubling both charge and distance gives net change of 2/4 = ½ the original force

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Voltage and Energy Are Not the Same Thing
topics: Electric potential (V) vs. electric potential energy (PE = qV)
Equipotential lines and their relationship to field lines
Work done moving charge: W = qΔV
lessons.examTip: Students say 'higher voltage means more energy' without specifying the charge — electric potential energy = qV; a proton and an electron at the same potential have equal |PE| but the proton's is positive and the electron's is negative

lessons.lessonTitle: How Resistors Control Current in Circuits
lessons.examTip: Students add resistors in parallel using the reciprocal formula but forget to take the final reciprocal — 1/Req = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ gives you 1/Req; you must take the reciprocal of that sum to get Req; the parallel combination is ALWAYS less than the smallest individual resistor

lessons.lessonTitle: How Moving Charges Create Magnetic Fields (and Vice Versa)
topics: Magnetic force on moving charge: F = qv × B (right-hand rule)
Force on current-carrying wire: F = IL × B
Magnetic field from long straight wire and solenoid
lessons.examTip: Students apply the right-hand rule without specifying the velocity direction of the charge — for negative charges, use the right-hand rule then REVERSE the direction; the magnetic force on an electron moving right in an upward B field points opposite to the force on a proton

lessons.lessonTitle: What It Means for a Relation to Be a Function
topics: Function notation: f(x) means output, not multiplication
lessons.examTip: Students write the range as all real numbers by default — the range is the set of ACTUAL OUTPUT values; always determine what y-values are actually achieved, not what's theoretically possible from the formula

lessons.lessonTitle: How Transformations Move and Reshape Graphs
topics: Stretches and compressions: af(x) and f(bx)
lessons.examTip: Students shift horizontally in the wrong direction — f(x − 3) shifts RIGHT 3 (not left); the sign inside the function is OPPOSITE to the direction of shift because you're replacing x with x−3, not adding 3 to x

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Inverse Functions Undo Each Other (And How to Find Them)
topics: Inverse function: swapping input and output
Finding f⁻¹(x) algebraically: swap x and y, solve
lessons.examTip: Students confuse f⁻¹(x) with 1/f(x) — f⁻¹(x) is the INVERSE FUNCTION (swap x and y); 1/f(x) is the RECIPROCAL; these are completely different; f(x) = 2x has f⁻¹(x) = x/2 but 1/f(x) = 1/(2x)

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Combine Functions and What That Means
lessons.examTip: Students evaluate f(g(x)) in the wrong order — (f∘g)(x) means apply g FIRST, then apply f to that result; they often compute g(f(x)) instead; always substitute the inner function result into the outer function

lessons.lessonTitle: Even, Odd, and Neither: Reading Symmetry Algebraically
topics: Even function: f(−x) = f(x) → y-axis symmetry
lessons.examTip: Students test only one x-value to determine even/odd — a function must satisfy f(−x) = f(x) for ALL x in its domain to be even; one counterexample disproves it; always simplify f(−x) fully before concluding

lessons.lessonTitle: What the End Behavior of a Polynomial Tells You Before You Graph
topics: Even/odd degree and positive/negative leading coefficient
lessons.examTip: Students determine end behavior from the first term written, not the leading term — the leading term is the HIGHEST degree term; if a polynomial is written in non-standard form, identify the highest degree term first

lessons.lessonTitle: How Multiplicity of Zeros Controls Bouncing vs. Crossing
topics: Roots with odd multiplicity: graph crosses x-axis
Roots with even multiplicity: graph touches and bounces
lessons.examTip: Students think double roots mean the graph barely crosses — a root with EVEN multiplicity means the graph TOUCHES but does not cross the x-axis; odd multiplicity means it CROSSES; multiplicity 1 = simple crossing

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Rational Functions Have Holes and Asymptotes (And Which Is Which)
topics: Vertical asymptotes vs. holes from factored form
Horizontal asymptote rules from degree comparison
lessons.examTip: Students make everything a vertical asymptote — a common factor that cancels creates a HOLE (removable discontinuity), not a vertical asymptote; the vertical asymptote comes from zeros of the denominator that DON'T cancel

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Divide Polynomials and Use the Remainder
lessons.examTip: Students apply synthetic division to divisors like (x + 3) without changing the sign — synthetic division uses c where the divisor is (x − c); for (x + 3), c = −3, not +3; entering +3 gives completely wrong results

lessons.lessonTitle: Finding All Zeros: The Full Rational Root Strategy
topics: Using synthetic division to test and deflate
Complex conjugate pairs and irreducible quadratics
lessons.examTip: Students stop after finding two real roots — the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra guarantees a degree-n polynomial has EXACTLY n roots (counting multiplicity) in the complex numbers; after finding real roots, check if remaining factor has complex roots

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Exponential Growth Eventually Beats Every Polynomial
topics: Exponential function f(x) = abˣ: base and growth/decay
Domain, range, and asymptote of exponential
Comparing linear, polynomial, and exponential growth rates
lessons.examTip: Students confuse exponential growth rate with percent increase — if b = 1.08, the growth rate is 8% PER PERIOD; the base directly encodes the growth factor, not the percent; b = 0.92 means 8% decay (1 − 0.92 = 0.08 = 8%)

lessons.lessonTitle: What a Logarithm Is Actually Asking
topics: Common log (base 10) and natural log (base e)
Graph of log as inverse of exponential
lessons.examTip: Students evaluate log_2(8) by calculating 2×8 or 8/2 — a logarithm asks 'what EXPONENT on the base gives this number?'; log_2(8) = 3 because 2³ = 8; always rewrite as the equivalent exponential equation to solve

lessons.lessonTitle: Logarithm Laws: Breaking Apart and Rebuilding Expressions
topics: Product: log(AB) = log A + log B
Quotient: log(A/B) = log A − log B
lessons.examTip: Students write log(A + B) = log A + log B — there is NO log law for the log of a sum; log(AB) = log A + log B (product rule applies to multiplication, NOT addition); this is the most common logarithm error

lessons.lessonTitle: Solving Exponential and Logarithmic Equations
topics: Isolating the exponential, then taking log of both sides
Checking for extraneous solutions in log equations
lessons.examTip: Students accept extraneous solutions in log equations — after solving, CHECK that the argument of EVERY log in the original equation is POSITIVE; log(negative number) is undefined, so solutions that make the argument ≤ 0 must be rejected

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Radians Are More Useful Than Degrees
topics: Arc length and sector area formulas: s = rθ, A = ½r²θ
lessons.examTip: Students use degree measures in s = rθ — this formula REQUIRES θ in RADIANS; using degrees gives wrong answers; always convert to radians before applying arc length or sector area formulas

lessons.lessonTitle: How the Unit Circle Encodes All Trig Values
topics: Unit circle: (cos θ, sin θ) at angle θ
Exact values at 0, π/6, π/4, π/3, π/2 and their multiples
lessons.examTip: Students memorize unit circle values without understanding reference angles — sin(5π/6) is not sin(5π/6) from scratch; 5π/6 is in Quadrant II with reference angle π/6; sin is positive in Q2, so sin(5π/6) = sin(π/6) = 1/2

lessons.lessonTitle: How Amplitude, Period, and Phase Shift Transform Trig Graphs
topics: y = A sin(Bx + C) + D: identifying each parameter
lessons.examTip: Students read phase shift as −C when it should be −C/B — for y = sin(2x − π), factor as sin(2(x − π/2)); phase shift is π/2 to the RIGHT, not π; always factor out B before reading the phase shift

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Inverse Trig Functions Have Restricted Ranges
topics: Why restrictions are necessary for invertibility
Solving trig equations on restricted vs. full domains
lessons.examTip: Students give all solutions when only the principal value is needed (or vice versa) — arcsin(x) returns ONE value in [−π/2, π/2]; when solving sin θ = 0.5 on [0, 2π], there are TWO solutions (π/6 and 5π/6); read the problem carefully for the domain

lessons.lessonTitle: Proving and Applying Trig Identities
topics: Pythagorean identities: sin²+cos²=1 and derived forms
lessons.examTip: Students 'prove' identities by cross-multiplying both sides — proofs must be one-directional; transform ONE side only until it equals the other; never operate on both sides simultaneously as if it's an equation to solve

lessons.lessonTitle: What Makes a Sequence Arithmetic or Geometric
lessons.examTip: Students apply arithmetic formula to geometric sequences — check: constant DIFFERENCE → arithmetic; constant RATIO → geometric; if successive terms multiply by the same factor, the sequence is geometric even if the terms grow rapidly

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Sum a Finite Arithmetic or Geometric Series
topics: Setting up the formula: finding n, a₁, aₙ or r
lessons.examTip: Students confuse n (number of terms) with aₙ (the nth term value) — n is the COUNT of terms; if terms run from a₁ to a₁₀₀, n = 100; to find n when terms are listed as values, use the nth term formula first

lessons.lessonTitle: When an Infinite Geometric Series Has a Finite Sum
lessons.examTip: Students apply S∞ = a₁/(1−r) when |r| > 1 — this formula is only valid when |r| < 1 (series CONVERGES); for |r| ≥ 1, the series diverges (sum grows without bound); always check |r| before applying the formula
